name: Glengarry Castle Hotel

tagline: David Bryce's 1866 Baronial mansion shares its Great Glen estate with the genuinely medieval ruin of Invergarry Castle, seat of the Clan MacDonell chiefs and twice visited by Bonnie Prince Charlie

description:
Glengarry Castle Hotel occupies a genuinely striking position on the shores of Loch Oich, in the heart of the Great Glen between Fort William and Inverness, and it offers something few Scottish castle-hotels can: two distinct historic buildings on one estate, each with its own separate story worth knowing before a visit. The hotel itself is Invergarry House, a substantial Scots Baronial mansion designed by David Bryce — the same prolific Victorian architect behind Glenapp Castle further south — and built between 1866 and 1869 for Edward Ellice Jr. Close to the estate's main entrance, and clearly visible from the access road, stands something considerably older: the ruined tower of Invergarry Castle itself, a genuinely medieval structure with a history stretching back centuries before Bryce ever put pen to paper.

Invergarry Castle was the seat of the chiefs of Clan MacDonell of Glengarry from the 15th century onward, a position that placed it squarely in the path of some of the most turbulent episodes in Highland history. In 1654, the castle was burned by Cromwellian troops under General Monck, part of the wider suppression of Highland clan power during the Commonwealth period. It was rebuilt and reoccupied, and nearly a century later found itself at the centre of events again during the Jacobite Rising of 1745: Bonnie Prince Charlie himself visited the castle twice, using it as a rallying point in the campaign that would end so decisively at Culloden. The castle paid a heavy price for that association — in the brutal aftermath of Culloden, it was burned once more, this time by the forces of the Duke of Cumberland, whose ruthless suppression of Jacobite sympathisers across the Highlands earned him the enduring nickname 'the Butcher.'

The ruin that survives today is exactly that: a shell, its interior unstable and fenced off for safety, but its walls and setting on a rocky outcrop above the loch remain genuinely evocative and are freely accessible to anyone exploring the estate grounds or driving in along the access road — no ticket, booking or hotel stay required. This is a meaningfully different situation from some other Scottish properties sharing a name or estate with an older ruin: rather than a source of confusion, Invergarry's ruin and its Victorian mansion sit together as two complementary attractions on the same piece of ground, each illuminating a different chapter of the glen's history.

Edward Ellice Jr., the mansion's original owner, died in 1934, and Invergarry House was eventually converted into Glengarry Castle Hotel in 1960, a name that deliberately invokes the older ruin's legacy even though the two buildings are physically distinct. The hotel today is an AA-rated 3-star country house hotel with a Rosette-recognised restaurant, its rooms looking out over Loch Oich and the surrounding grounds — landscaped parkland that itself forms part of the visiting experience, with mature trees and lochside walks connecting the two historic structures.

For travellers making their way along the Great Glen — the dramatic geological fault line running from Fort William to Inverness via Loch Ness — Glengarry offers a rare combination: a comfortable, historically grounded base for the night, and a genuine piece of clan history to explore on foot before checking in, entirely free of charge and open at any hour.

The wider Invergarry area carries additional layers of Jacobite-era history worth knowing for anyone drawn to the estate's own story: the village sits close to routes used repeatedly during both the 1715 and 1745 risings, and the broader MacDonell clan lands surrounding Loch Oich and Loch Garry saw some of the heaviest reprisals in the Highland suppression that followed Culloden. Walking the ruin's grounds today, with Loch Oich stretching out below and the mountains of the Great Glen rising on either side, it is easy to understand why this particular stretch of ground mattered enough to be fought over, burned and rebuilt more than once across four centuries.
history: Invergarry Castle was the seat of the chiefs of Clan MacDonell of Glengarry from the 15th century. It was burned by Cromwellian troops under General Monck in 1654, then rebuilt and reoccupied. During the Jacobite Rising of 1745, the castle was visited twice by Bonnie Prince Charlie, and in the aftermath of the Battle of Culloden it was burned again by forces under the Duke of Cumberland. The ruin survives on the same estate as the current hotel building, Invergarry House, a Scots Baronial mansion designed by architect David Bryce and built 1866–69 for Edward Ellice Jr. Ellice died in 1934, and the mansion was converted into Glengarry Castle Hotel in 1960.

faqs.question: Can I visit the ruins of Invergarry Castle without staying at the hotel?
faqs.answer: Yes. The ruined tower of Invergarry Castle stands on the hotel's estate near the main entrance and is freely visible and accessible from the grounds and access road at any time, with no ticket or booking required. The interior of the ruin is fenced off for safety due to its unstable structure, but the exterior and setting above Loch Oich can be explored on foot as part of any visit to the estate.

faqs.question: Is Glengarry Castle Hotel the same building as the ruined Invergarry Castle?
faqs.answer: No — they are two physically distinct buildings on the same estate. The hotel occupies Invergarry House, a Scots Baronial mansion built in 1866–69 by architect David Bryce, while the ruined Invergarry Castle is a genuinely medieval tower house standing separately near the estate's entrance, with its own much older history as the seat of Clan MacDonell of Glengarry.

faqs.question: Why was Invergarry Castle burned more than once?
faqs.answer: The castle was burned by Cromwellian troops under General Monck in 1654 during the suppression of Highland clan power, and again after the Battle of Culloden in 1746 by forces under the Duke of Cumberland, in retaliation for the castle's role as a rallying point for Bonnie Prince Charlie during the 1745 Jacobite Rising, which the prince visited twice.
